utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, assisted today and for the rest of this week by Jasmina Bosnjakovic, as Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm no longer used to making the appearances for my team because Mr. Zecevic has been doing it so far. On behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and the Case Manager, Tatjana Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence today appearing, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- if there are no preliminary matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are, I mentioned that to your Legal Officer. Your Honour, I'm afraid there are a number of matters. First, can I formally apply to have exhibited the three pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- you said a number of matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They're all short, Your Honour, but they need to be dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this one simply so that I don't forget. The pages of the -- the three pages of the interview that I put to Mr. Vlaski in cross-examination, there was a discussion when Mr. Hannis was in court. And all I want to do is it ask that those three pages, which are pages 30 to 32 of the interview, Exhibit 9020, as the 65 ter number, be made exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Position of, I believe, both Defence teams are the following. We object to this approach of our learned friend Ms. Korner on the following basis. First of all, witness left. Secondly, on the basis of Mr. Hannis submission, I believe it was on Friday, or Thursday, the main issue and the position of the Prosecution is that they were, to some extent, unsecure, whether Ms. Korner rightly quoted particular questions and gists of Mr. Vlaski interview. And our position is that everything is fine. Ms. Korner rightly quoted these particular questions, and his answers. Ms. Korner got her time and the chance, and that's over. End of story. It is great concern of the Defence that, if this practice will be allowed, this practice of Prosecution will be allowed by Trial Chamber, that would actually create a sort of practice of introducing on the back door certain documents or exhibits, et cetera. So, in short, this is position of Defence team, and we strongly object to have these few pages admitted as the exhibit, because, as I said, the basis was whether Ms. Korner rightly quoted and interpreted these particular portions or not. And we say yes, everything was fine, transcript is clear, end of story. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I thought this matter had been settled from last week, and the -- it was -- when this issue had been canvassed it was fairly clear that the relevant portions having been put to the witness by you in -- was it -- I think in re-examination that that was sufficient. Why -- I -- I'm not sure I understand why this issue is being resurrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... about whether I'd quoted correctly, I happened to read the transcript, and there was an argument of whether I was asking for the whole interview or just the three pages. And I'm just asking for the three pages to be made an exhibit, in the same way as if a document had been read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honours, it's hearing on 18th of February, which is Thursday. If are you looking for this particular parts. In fact, Mr. Hannis mentioned that on Friday, this position, and he said, well, Ms. Korner wasn't there, and he will wait for Monday. But actually, this particular, I would say, line of questioning was on Thursday. It's page -- well, I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I found Thursday. At page 6499, and as everybody rightly says, Mr. Hannis was dealing with this. And Judge Harhoff said: "Maybe the Prosecution should simply just specify exactly which parts you wish to have exhibited." Whether it's any of the parts read out or the pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'm just asking for the pages, as I would do with any other document that was read in full. And I cannot see what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we will give our ruling in the course of today's sitting but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that's fine. Thank you very much. Your Honour, can I move to a second matter, and that's this question of -- of late notification, if you like, of exhibits and application to add to the 65 ter. Obviously I'm aware of what took place in respect of Mr. Hannis's witness last week. Can I say something about the situation. These witnesses, most of them, have only -- were interviewed sometime ago. When they come up here, and that's before we did our 65 ter list, we simply don't have the budget to go and re-interview everybody. For example, today's witness was interviewed in 2001. To go and re-interview everybody well in advance of when they're being called. When they come, they look at documents to see whether they can recognise them or say something which is there to assist the Trial Chamber. So quite often, as in this particular case, and indeed as with Mr. Hannis's witness, we won't know until the day before the trial -- the day before the trial, the day before the witness is called, whether they can say something useful about a particular document which is not on our 65 ter list or may be on our 65 ter list but hasn't been shown to him before. We would love this to be a perfect system and so we'd be able to notify everyone well in advance of which documents the witness can speak to but it just logically isn't possible. And we know that Your Honours have well in mind the fact that the interests of justice are paramount in this case and that Your Honours use such evidence as you can to find the truth. So, Your Honours, with apologies, always -- and we always do notify the Defence in advance, we cannot always have the perfect list of documents. In today's case, that has proved to be exactly the same. We notified the Defence last Friday and Your Honours of the documents we may be using. As it turns out, because some he can't identify, we won't be using all of them. But what we're asking is not to have to put in a written motion, which would be the day before, simply to deal with the documents, unless they are documents that have never been disclosed, and that's a completely different matter and I'm not talking about that today except with one exception, a map. That we're allowed to deal with it, we MFI it and then we apply formally in motion, as we have just recently done, to add the document to our 65 ter list. As I say I know it is not perfect, but it seems to me that it is not unfair, if I can put it that way, to the Defence, provided we give notice and provided those documents have been disclosed. And for these purposes I'm not talking about -- obviously re-examination. Can I -- that leads me into the next problem, I'm afraid, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before you move on, could I just ask how this presentation of documents is organised? Because what I imagine takes place is that in the process leading up to the witness's arrival to The Hague, the Prosecutor who is dealing with this witness will review the material and select the documents that -- that will then be put to the witness once the witness arrives, and in your proofing session, will be shown to him. Now, some of these documents, you say, he doesn't recognise. He has never seen them before, unable to speak to them. While others he may.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And -- and so you end up with a number of documents which -- to which the witness can actually speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Some of these documents, you then say, may not have been put on your 65 ter list. So my question is now, whether it would be possible to, first of all, notify the Defence, way ahead of the witness's arrival, that these are the documents that you actually intend to throw at him when -- or her, when she comes. Because that would at least provide some degree of earlier notice to the Defence and also to the Chamber for us to prepare, and -- and that might solve some of the problem of notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we appreciate that and that's clearly -- now having seen the problems, we're trying to do that. Up till now the problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As the Presiding Judge said, we will deal with this in the break and offer our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I say it leads me into, I'm afraid, what is a problem and that's -- which I alluded to, I think, last week. Today's witness, there are huge -- as you have seen from the list, a large number of documents that it became clear that he might be able to speak to, not to mention having to listen to his interview and also to some intercepts. Arrangements were made for Defence counsel to see him --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, please. Please, Ms. Korner. Your Honours, would it be appropriate to hear submission of the Defence on the previous issue before you go to another issue. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just have a few things to say. I want to point out to you what kind of difficulties the Defence is facing with this type of application by the Prosecution. Since the Defence based its preparations on -- based on the 65 ter list and the summaries of witness evidence, our investigation and our preparations were geared in that direction. Unless the Prosecution makes an application with reasonable notice, leaving enough time for the Defence to check certain documentation and to conduct certain inquiries on the ground and prepare to deal with such documents, including changes in the strategy, if necessary, we are very prejudiced. Introducing new documentation just two days before the arrival of a witness causes us enormous difficulties, and regardless of the formal equality of arms between the two sides, we have much less resources, much less people to be able to prepare adequately for the trial, and that is an objective problem. In this situation, we can either ask for a delay in calling the particular witness; or we can ask for the witness to be re-called later, which poses certain difficulties for everyone, including the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution had foresight, they had intentions, a -- particular intentions when calling a particular witness. By doing this, they are enlarging the scope of evidence. I think the Trial Chamber should take that into account when deciding on an application like this, especially since some documents are included that have not even been disclosed to the Defence. And I know that the Trial Chamber will decide to what extent they are relevant to the proceedings, but I just wanted to the point out these few aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, my -- my initial question and I don't want to argue, I just want to try to understand, was why are these documents, whether the particular witness can speak to them or not, why are they not on -- on your initial or initially on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a perfectly fair question. There's a number of reasons. One is that the Prosecution was -- I wouldn't say ordered because I don't think it was an order exactly but was asked to cut down its 65 ter list way, way back, when the Trial Chamber was differently constituted, and this was before - I think we're going back to 2007 or 2008, I can't off the top of my head remember - before Zupljanin was arrested. Then, having done that, when it came to looking at what was to go onto the 65 ter list, the feeling was that still then that we ought to restrict it as much as possible particularly with adjudicated facts. The third reason was that the issues which have become live issues in this case, like communication, for example, were never made clear until after the 65 ter list was served and indeed wasn't even made clear in the pre-trial brief in many respects from the Defence, and the issues are now coming to light which means we have got do deal with them. And so that's -- that's the -- it's a mixture of reasons, I accept. But that's the reality of the situation. As I say, it is completely different matter if we haven't disclosed, and I hear my learned friend saying we haven't disclosed. I am unaware of any documents, other than the map of Sarajevo which I produced this morning because it became apparent that the one didn't have Lukavica in it, that we haven't disclosed. So, Your Honours, I appreciate it is not ideal. And can I say straightaway we -- it is clear that -- that we're going to have to try and find the resources to put together the packages for the witnesses before this. I -- can I assure Your Honours that, like the Defence, we're buried in work at the moment. And -- but I absolutely accept that the longer the time we can give notice to you and to the Defence, the better. And we will try and work out a system. The only thing at the moment that I wanted to raise was just simply that -- this having to put into writing. I don't think it assists anybody, either us nor indeed you the Trial Judges, to have further written applications which you have to deal with, and so that is the matter that I wanted to raise. But I can just explain also my concern about witnesses. The gentleman who is about to come, as I say, got here on Saturday night. He was seen for two hours on Saturday morning by the Defence because as has been explained to you, the Defence don't have the resources to see the witnesses in advance. He then sat there until 6.00 in the evening when he informed us that the Defence wanted to speak to him again, that evening, which they did, for another two hours. So he hadn't finished going through the documents and -- and this is our witness. He had to come back in again this morning, finish looking through the documents. In fact I saw him for a total, I think, of 45 minutes in the end. Leaving that aside and the fact that he is a Prosecution witness, it is oppressive, in our view, to put somebody through that sort of interrogation, and it's not what the Defence being entitled to speak to Defence witness -- Prosecution witnesses is meant to be. So -- I -- in fact, I spoke to the witness and asked him if he wasn't too exhausted to give evidence this afternoon. He says, no, he's perfectly happy to go, as far as we can see. But this cannot not be right, Your Honours. Which leads me -- and it's connected with the problems about giving advance notice to the Defence of which -- to which documents the witness can speak, if such time as he's brought up here, the Defence -- a good half of his time was taken up by the Defence today, with this witness, which we say is wrong. Additionally, Your Honour, we had an e-mail today from the Defence Zupljanin. The witness who is coming after this witness, this week, was contacted by us at the request of the Defence who provided a list of those witnesses they wished to talk to. Nearly all of them are -- we're in open session. But, anyhow, this particular witness said that he did not wish to talk to the Defence. He also said he did not wish to have his contact details passed to the Defence, because they were asked that as well. That was in October of last year. His Honour Judge Harhoff may remember -- or Your Honours may remember. And that was the arrangement, that we would contact the witnesses. There would be no direct contact from the Defence. We are informed today that the investigator for the Zupljanin team got in touch with this witness, how we don't know, who has now allegedly changed his mind about speaking to the Defence. Now the system has been that we ask -- if they -- if we are re-asked, when the witness gets here we ask them, Are you prepared to talk to us, or if the Defence notifies they'd like the witness to be asked again we're prepared to do it. We are deeply troubled by a Defence investigator, most of whom are ex-MUP officers of one kind or another, speaking to a witness whom they have been told does not wish to speak to them. And Your Honours I am in regard to the question of timing, and -- and Mr. Cvijetic seeing this witness for so long, I don't think that is something we may have to bring back before Your Honours. We really have to bring the witnesses out so much earlier, but I am concerned and I am asking Your Honours for a ruling that the Defence do not send their investigators to speak to witnesses who have said, in terms, they do not wish to speak to the Defence. That's -- it seems to me that that's something that is inappropriate, if I can put it that way. Your Honours, before I move on to my last point which I need go into closed session -- private session for. I don't know whether there wants to be a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just before we respond, which witness is Ms. Korner saying that I have been in contact for a long time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness who is about to start giving evidence, two hours yesterday morning and two hours last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Yesterday morning, between 9.00 and 11.15, and yesterday evening between 7.30 and 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I thought that you were discussing all the time some future witness. This one I met here. I thought we were talking about a future witness. Yes, it is correct that we met yesterday with the knowledge of the Victims and Witness Service and both these encounters were attended by representatives of the VWS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to explain the position of the Defence, with regard to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Next witness. He is a viva voce -- it's open so can we mention his name, just for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does it matter? Is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's not -- it's not necessary --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't mean the witness who's about to start --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- this afternoon. The one after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No problem. So for the next witness we have, first of all, understanding that there is no so-called -- so-called right to have a witness. There is no kind of restriction in our road to justice for each side to have exclusive right on the witness. Of course, Defence is very, very mindful regarding the position of witness, whether particular witness in question would like or don't like to speak with Defence. That's completely understandable. In -- in this particular case, we have information, because this witness is chief of the one of the departments in CSB Banja Luka and former colleague of our investigator so they have a good relationship, private and professional, and when -- and, of course, they -- they made several contacts well before. And last contact, when our learned friend from Prosecution informed us, surprisingly, that next witness doesn't want to speak with the Defence, our investigators checked that fact. Maybe it was a misunderstanding in communication. And finally we got the position that the witness said, I don't want to be Prosecution witness, and I don't want to be Defence witness. Some -- something to that extent. Obviously that he doesn't understand in which capacity he is -- he is calling. But, in any case, he never mentioned that he don't -- he doesn't want to speak with the Defence. That's the point. That's the bottom line. So Variant A, maybe Prosecution in its communications with the officer in field and the other members of -- of Prosecution office did not understand this position of the witness. And the other, which I really don't believe, is that simply Prosecution tried to manipulate and to misinterpret certain situation. Simply as that. Point number one, that next witness never expressed his will not to speak with the Defence. As far as I'm informed, his position is that he even don't want to be a Prosecution witness, or Defence. I'm not going into these details. But at the end of the day, Defence would like to have a clear situation. We do not want to rely upon the informations regarding witnesses from Prosecution side. We want, in presence of our authorised member of the team, whether in the field or here, to have a clear word from the -- from the witness, No, I don't want to speak with the Defence, because, otherwise, it's a huge and waste and -- and great, I would say, space for misunderstanding or misinterpretation, et cetera, et cetera. So I don't have any problem for -- for this Trial Chamber to rule and to give certain guide-lines or instructions with regard to the witnesses. Of course, having in mind the fact that a witness is not a property of the either party. A witness is a witness. But if that would be the case, I don't have any problem that, for each particular witness in this situation where we don't have clear position and answers between two parties, that the witness himself or herself will be able to say yes or no. Yes, I want to speak with Defence; no, I don't want to speak with Defence, in the presence of the member of -- of Defence team. And, of course, all witnesses are witnesses of the Court, and we are all going on this road to justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole point about all of this was that witnesses should not be pressurised, particularly witnesses who are ex-members of the MUP, and should be free to decide whether or not they wish to speak to the Defence. All that we're saying is, it is improper for an investigator to ring up a witness who they have been told does not wish to speak to them nor does he want his contact details. Nobody has explained how he got his contact details but -- and what we're saying is that the Defence, if they think there's a mistake being made, are perfectly entitled and we're perfectly happy to make the phone call in front of them so they can hear what the witness has said. But they should not behind the -- as it were, in a havey-cavey manner, ringing up these witnesses. Now, Your Honours, until the witness arrives we can't sort this out. But as I say, my concern is that undue pressure is both being put on the witnesses by the fact of the Defence seeing them. As I've said over and over again, if the Defence want to interview witnesses, the proper way for them to do it is to interview them using an investigator or themselves somewhere before the -- not immediately before the witness gives evidence. That's the first thing. Second thing. If they don't accept what the witness has told us, we're perfectly happy for a further phone call to be made to the witnesses in the presence of the Defence, asking them whether they want to speak to them. But, Your Honour, that -- that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in terms of this last issue, we will -- we have the benefit of what counsel on both sides have said and we will be assisted by the transcript and decide whether it would be practical and useful for the Chamber to attempt, in the light of established practice of the Tribunal, to give the type of guide-lines which both sides seem to suggest would be helpful. You had a third matter, Ms. Korner, which you want to go into --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I do apologise, Your Honour, just a very short submission. We strongly object to the use of word of "pressurised" or "pressure." It is not fair. It is not true. It's not the case. There is no pressure. It is not fair from you to use that word. In any case, we are ready to have any statement of the witness to say whether he was pressurised or threatened or whatever and then we can deal with that. We have rules here. It is not fair to put these kind of [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would prefer not to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- down that road. Could we go into private session to deal with Ms. Korner's last matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You're ready with your Witness 164.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exactly. Your Honours, while he's being sought -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While he's being sought we -- or got, we asked for three hours originally. It is quite clear, even though the number of documents he can deal with is not as great as those on the list, that it's going to take a little time just to take him through the documents. Your Honours, I'm hoping that I have got some time in the bank from having cut short my examination of Mr. Vlaski, and so could ask that I be given four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think the way we approached this in the past is we will see how your three hours go, and towards the end of that, then we'll entertain your application.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we thank you for your appearance and attendance before the Tribunal, and I will begin by asking you your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Drago Borovcanin. I was born on the 20th of July, 1948, in Mokro. That is a small village near Pale. If necessary, I can give you further details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a professor of sociology. That is not my current line of work, but I did get a degree from the faculty of political science at the University of Sarajevo, and my degree was in sociology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your current line of work is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I work in the Ministry for Human Rights and Refugees of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is one of the nine ministries that were established after the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed. Right now, I am working at that ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or in your -- your country of residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never before. This is my very first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would begin by explaining to you briefly the procedure that is followed in this Tribunal, and which is fairly common in terms of courts universally. That is that the side calling you will begin - in this case, it is the Prosecution - by asking you questions, and then the counsel for each of the two accused, if they wish, would have questions themselves of you. The Prosecution would then have an opportunity to ask you questions again, and the Chamber, if it considers it appropriate, arising out of those comments, would -- may itself have questions of you. You are -- it is expected that your testimony would extend over the next three days, and the hours of sitting at the Tribunal are essentially four hours per day, with two 20-minute breaks during those four hours. The -- I would not invite counsel for the Prosecution, Ms. Korner, to begin her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just -- Your Honour, he did take the oath, did he, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, I want to deal, first of all, with how you come to be a witness in the case. I think you were interviewed on the 14th of August, 2007; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a witness.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: As a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And during the course of that interview, did you give replies to the investigator's questions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did give replies to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yesterday -- I think you arrived in The Hague on Saturday evening. Did you spend two hours yesterday morning with Mr. Cvijetic and another of the Defence lawyers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I spent a certain amount of time with them. I'm not sure whether it was exactly two hours. I wasn't really paying that much attention but it could be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And apart from Mr. Cvijetic, was it Mr. Krgovic who was present? The gentleman sitting behind you -- over there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then yesterday evening, did you spend a further - I think you told the investigator this morning - two hours with Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That would be it roughly because we were supposed to meet at 1700 hours and then we spent a bit more time before that with our colleagues, the investigators of the OTP, and then we met up at the hotel, and then we talked roughly about that same amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now can we deal with your background, just in a short period of time, please. In fact -- I'm sorry, there's one other question. In fact, by the time you spoke to the investigators in August of 2007, had you already been contacted by lawyers or investigators representing Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Not until then, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you were interviewed by the OTP, didn't you tell them in interview that you had been contacted indirectly and unofficially, as you put it, by people representing Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But that was over the telephone. I thought that your question pertained to direct contacts. Over the telephone they did ask me whether I wanted to be a Defence witness. I remained ambiguous on that, as the interview says. I said give me time to think about it. I said neither yes nor no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Well, now let's move very briefly, please, to your background. Is it right - you told the Judges when you were born - that you started work for the MUP in the mid-1970s, around 1975?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: March 1974, that's when I started working for the Ministry of the Interior. At that time what was organised was a type of seminar or course, lasting five or six months, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I was leaving out your training. Actual -- all right. But March 1974, and did you start work in the -- the cities of Sarajevo SUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: After completing the course, yes. Yes. Relatively short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then did you work as a republic inspector?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: After that, no. After that, I was transferred from the SUP of the city of Sarajevo, as it was called at the time, to the Republican Secretariat of the Interior. That was the top institution of that kind in the former Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then I missed a part out, or the interview did. Did you, however, work as an inspector of police stations from about 1985?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I was in that line of work for a few years. Four years, was it? Perhaps a bit more than that. I really cannot remember because after that I was moved to another job, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, let's -- I tell you what, let's leave out your other jobs because I don't know that they are particularly relevant. But by 1991, were you appointed as chief of the operational duty in the CSB in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Sometime during that period, I was commander of the company for providing security for high-ranking persons, and then I was moved to the centre of Security Services in Sarajevo, and I was in charge of duty operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you tell us what that job entailed, being in charge of the duty operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is an operative position where people worked in shifts. That is to say, we worked night shifts as well. There were five of us who took turns there. The work itself meant that we monitored security-related developments in the area of the centre of security that we worked in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Where was the CSB located in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The CSB was located in the old part of Sarajevo, if I can put it that way. The street was Augusta Cesarca. We worked in that particular building and, of course, the other services were there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the next question I wanted to ask you. Which other services were in that building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I know that when the CSB was founded, we entered the building where the SUP of the city of Sarajevo had operated until then. I cannot tell you exactly on which basis offices were allocated to different services and departments. I know that our offices were on the ground floor, just like the communications people. And then there was the first floor and the second floor, where the city officials were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So in the same building was also the -- if you like, the -- the SUP of Sarajevo, the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not sure whether all the services could have been there. Perhaps some of them were elsewhere too. Quite simply, I have forgotten by now, so I cannot give you a full answer to your question, but I know that part of it was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now we know that in 1991, Mico Stanisic was appointed as secretary to the SUP of the city of Sarajevo. Did you ever meet him during the 1991 period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the position of secretary of the SUP? In the hierarchy of the SUP, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, as for the city SUP itself, that was the top person, yes. Perhaps top manager would be the right word. In the city SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And would the top person in the city SUP be reporting directly to the minister, or the assistant minister, or would he reporting to the chief of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I was asked that earlier on. I was asked that by you too, in part. I just know that the republican SUP was the top institution, and I thought the communications with them were more frequent, and it was their duty to report to them. As for the CSB, I don't think that we exchanged information in the course of our official duties, ex officio. For example, that they were duty-bound to report to us about something, but, at any rate, there was cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you say you never met Mico Stanisic in 1991. Did you meet him before he came minister of the interior of the Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. Until he was appointed minister of the interior of the Republika Srpska, I never had occasion to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you remain as chief of the operation in the CSB in Sarajevo until after the conflict started in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Until then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once the conflict started, and after the split in the MUP, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I would need some time to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can do it fairly shortly that would be a help.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I'll try. So, I was working in that CSB, in the operations duty service, and, of course, all sorts of information was coming in from all sides, and there was a psychosis, a fear reigning in town. People were forming various groups and it was very still among my colleagues. Nobody wanted -- seemed to want to open this Pandora's box. And then in April, that means before the war started, it one of the night shifts, I believe it was the last night shift, a group of armed men who we didn't know burst in. They had automatic guns. I was taken aback, afraid, and asked, Who are you? And they said, We are the ones asking questions here. They were wearing uniforms and on the shoulder of one of them I saw the lettering, "Patriotic League," and that was a message to me. We had automatic weapons ourselves handy in the service, but it would have been stupid to try anything. It was a message to me and my colleagues that things were going haywire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sorry. I don't quite follow this. They burst in, said they were the Patriotic League. What happened then? Did they take over the CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They did not say they were members of the Patriotic League. I just noticed "Patriotic League" written on a shoulder patch. And when I asked who they were, they simply said, We are the ones asking questions here. They went upstairs to the communication centres while we were left downstairs. I can't say that we were disarmed completely but it would have been stupid to do anything, to try to get hold of our weapons, because they were -- they looked rather serious and very intimidating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Borovcanin. I'm still trying to understand. Are you saying at that stage you were all expelled from the CSB or that these men simply came in, went upstairs and then left again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They just passed through the building. How long they were inside and what they were doing, I couldn't see because they were upstairs. But they did go to the communication centre, which means that they had a good reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did they then -- after they had been to the communication centre, did they leave or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. The communication centre was upstairs. We remained in our offices, myself, the junior operations duty officer, and the signalsmen who were working in our department. Nobody left the office. These people stayed upstairs in the building for a while. They -- I don't know what they were doing there. Then they went downstairs, got into their cars and were gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all that I was trying to get at. All right. So -- all right -- yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then move to -- you actually then did leave, did you not, the CSB in Sarajevo, because there was, at that stage, a Serbian MUP, as apart from the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know of any Serbian MUP in that period. That's -- this is the first time I hear of it, from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: But let me go to back what you just said a moment ago. Very soon afterwards we had a working meeting with the leader in the centre, Mr. Bakir Alispahic, and I raised the question, Who were these people who burst in on us? What kind of police are we? I believe that everyone in my place would have considered that a huge problem and raised it at the first possible meeting. And he told me, I'm surprised to hear these words from you as a police officer. They are members of the reserve force of the state security. I was not naive enough to believe that but I understood the message, and the message was that I was no longer secure in my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pause there, please, Mr. Borovcanin. And, if necessary, I'm sure the Defence will ask you further questions about all of this. You just said you were unaware of the split in the MUP. Are you telling us that you didn't know about the telegram that Mr. Mandic had sent on 31st of March, making -- which made it clear that there was now a Serbian MUP in Bosnia as well as the old republic MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That document, the dispatch was not known to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's forget about whether you knew about the split or not. Is it right that you left the Sarajevo CSB and transferred, if we can put it that way, to the -- the Republika Srpska MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: We seem to have skipped a short period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I returned to my apartment in the neighbourhood of the Mojmilo and then came the meeting that I just mentioned, when I asked Mr. Alispahic that question. But before that there is one incident that I should --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: -- tell you about here for the sake of completeness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin -- yes --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: -- and the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If you are -- if you -- if this incident you want to tell us is relevant to you leaving the MUP of Bosnia and going to the RS MUP, then, by all means do so. But only if it is relevant to that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Certainly, it's relevant. I got into my own car. I went to the meeting. And then at an intersection in the neighbourhood of Mojmilo I was intercepted by strangers, armed, who asked for my ID. They opened my boot, asked me who I was. I showed them my ID. I said I was a member of the MUP and they asked to see my weapons. Before that there had been several cases already when policemen were disarmed in a similar way, and therefore I said I had no weapons on me because if I had said otherwise, they would have disarmed me. They were certainly criminals. I said the weapon is in my office. And they looked very disappointed that they hadn't got anything off me. And I was allowed to go on my way. And that was the second incident that was a warning to me that I was unsafe and that I should worry about the safety of my family. Let me not even mention that there was fire opened at the windows of my apartment. I had many concerns for my safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Borovcanin. I understand your concerns for your safety. All I want to do is to get you, metaphorically speaking, to the time when you began work for the Serbian CSB. Did you begin -- were you appointed to work in the CSB, the Serbian CSB of Sarajevo which was called the Romanija-Birac CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Not immediately. Because, you see, large numbers of Serbs were leaving Sarajevo at the time. Anyone who had family elsewhere or family estates went there, to safer places. And sometime in April, I too went to my birth place, stayed there for two or three days, watching television carefully and reading newspapers to keep abreast of what was going on, and then I decided to go to the police station in Pale because - and you have to try to understand this - it was a time when any Serb fit to serve in the army who had failed to report to the MUP or the military department would be stigmatised, or at least looked down upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, I said to you, did I not, something like two hours ago that I had limited time to take you in evidence and that it would help if you just answer my question and don't volunteer information. Did you start work in around May of 1992 for the CSB, the Serbian CSB, of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. After reporting to the Pale police, we headed for Vrace. At that time, they were in the process of establishing the Security Services Centre because everything was done on a shoestring, you understand. And for several days I worked as inspector in that centre, which was only in the process of being established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. However, in May of 1992, did you start work -- I'm sorry. Were you appointed to the CSB, Serbian CSB, of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And your job was as what, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago. At the beginning, all the work that an inspector normally does, and that's the work I did at the time, implied touring police stations on the ground, getting insight into their work and performance, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you in fact become the chief of administration within the CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, after working as an inspector for I don't know how long, maybe a month, maybe less, I can't remember the date when I was appointed chief of police at the Security Services Centre. It could have been end May, or early June. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And whereabouts was the Serbian CSB based for the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, for a short while, in Vrace. But when snipers started targeting us, we realised we were not safe and we relocated to Lukavica, which is in the eastern part of Sarajevo, opposite the science and mathematical faculty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told us it was also in Vrace. Is that where the police school was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just look, please, briefly, if there is no objection from the Defence, to a map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This wasn't in our 65 ter list. No. Thank you. That's 10282. It's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- I can't see the darn thing. Okay. I think if we look towards the bottom of the map, we can see Lukavica, is that right, with sort of purple buildings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go -- I don't know if somebody's attempting to do something with the cursor, but it's -- it's in the middle of the map. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, purple buildings. I believe those was administrations of Energoinvest, the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, to make a long story short.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, can you tell us, can we see Vrace on the map?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, we should follow the road, the yellow road. Could you zoom out again? Vrace is not far from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Borovcanin. If you touch the screen it zooms around. So if you can indicate, just by touching the screen, if we can see Vrace, which I think we can, but I have lost it myself.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: All right, I'm sorry. Well, around here somewhere. You see the road leading from the Energoinvest company to the intersection. And then follow that road to the right. And this overpass leading to the centre of the city, that's -- that's Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So that was in the hills; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: It's not really a hill. It's a kind of saddle-shaped area that that separates Lukavica from the eastern part of Sarajevo. It stretches -- this area stretches almost all the way to the Mojmilo neighbourhood. It is perhaps one kilometre, two kilometres long, this saddle-shaped area that separates the urban part from the less populated part called Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think that's all we need for the moment. Thank you very much, sir. Next --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know where we are on the break. I'm always unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then I think if we can take it now, because I want him to look at the -- the chart. Oh, yes, Your Honours, may I ask that that map now become an exhibit. I don't think there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P986, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it is not objection, but I really don't see the purpose of this map. Maybe it will be better after the break for witness to -- to show or to put some marks or -- otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he has explained where Lukavica -- but I suppose it might help if he marked it. Perhaps he can do that now before it goes off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I mean, we know where it is but for the sake of Trial Chamber maybe it would be fair to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is always the site visit, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a pen and just mark, first of all, Lukavica, and then Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The map needs to be shrunk again. It's in -- I'm sorry, it's now too close.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it is still not showing Lukavica. It is still not showing Lukavica. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... needs to be lowered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just draw a circle, first of all, around Lukavica, and mark that 1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Oh ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now could you show us where Vrace is. Let's just put 1 -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Right. Just a second. This road -- this area here. Roughly this area. This is the -- these are the narrow confines of Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Short of crossed by -- by the road that leads to Grbavica. That's the urban part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in fact if one focuses in, one can just see -- under the line he has drawn you can actually see the name. Right. Does that need to be given a separate exhibit number? It probably does. Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the annotated map will be Exhibit P987.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. [Overlapping speakers] ... time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the break now and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... in connection with what I was saying about the witness, we had a -- an e-mail from the Witness and Victims Unit saying that the witness, last night, was exhausted and stressed. I did ask him today whether he felt all right to go on and he said yes. But I'm wondering whether Your Honours may think it's right to perhaps cut things a little bit short today and perhaps give your rulings at the end of the session. I think he really did have too much yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would it helpful if we were to inquire directly with the witness as to what his --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour may but it may well be that he feels that it is a matter of honour that you don't say you feel tired. Your Honour, I should add that I was -- entirely my fault, I was unaware of it, but someone who was aware of it -- there is in fact an order directed only to Stanisic dating back to 2005 saying they must not contact witnesses, Prosecution witnesses without written notice to us first. And, of course, it doesn't apply to Zupljanin, because he wasn't there. So -- and can I say straightaway, I don't want to suggest that in any way Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Pantelic were behaving improperly. I'm simply saying that, as a matter of reality, being contacted like that can be pressure and may comprise the witness's feeling of security. Anyhow, but, Your Honours, perhaps if we could deal with all these matters at the end of the day which would give the witness perhaps a chance not to have to go on to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: May I have the assistance of counsel in terms of your last suggestion. We ordinarily would -- the -- well, we're starting the 4.00 part of the session late for reasons that I will explain shortly. But we would go -- we would ordinarily go to 5.20 and then resume at 5.40 to 7.00. Is there a suggestion as to what time we should release the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was thinking if we could -- I don't know whether we have to take the break at -- was it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean that would be -- but if we could sort of carry on till, say, quarter to 6.00. You see, he was with us this morning because he hadn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I'm aware of the problem that you're trying to identify. So you're suggesting that we go to, say, 5.45 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and then release him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then release him and deal with whatever matters are -- there are to deal with. If that's satisfactory to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yeah. Everything is fine with us, of course. Just a few words in response to Ms. Korner, her submission on page 34, line 21 to 25. It is a well-known fact that we have certain impressions from Prosecution witnesses, so-called insiders, that they were pressed by -- I would say strange approach by Prosecution to them, considering them as suspects. And we have a numerous facts with that regard, that they were under stress during this -- giving statement to OTP -- to Office of the Prosecutor, and that I believe this practice, although we are now almost near the exit strategy, will not happen again. But, again, we are going to ask a number of witnesses with regard to their personal feelings when they were summoned as suspect, and then, during the statement, they're changed status, et cetera, et cetera. So in practice is also, I would say, of certain importance, to be -- think about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. So we will have the -- if the usher will escort the witness back to the stand, and I will deal with these -- our views on the three matters raised by Ms. Korner when the witness would be released at 5.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, Ms. Korner. Sir, I would have explained to you when you began your evidence as to the sequence in which matters would go. One of the things that I would have said that trials are fairly standard all over the world, and one of the standard features of trials all over the world is that the flow of evidence is often interrupted by a Court having to deal with procedural matters, and that is one of the reasons why the break that we took a while ago has been somewhat extended. Now that we are back on track, the rest of the day will proceed as follows. Ms. Korner will resume her examination-in-chief of you now. It's 5 -- it's now 4.36, and at 5.45, which will be in an hour and roughly ten minutes, you would be excused as a witness for the remainder of day, with the direction to return here tomorrow morning for 9.00. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, we'd reached the stage where you were the chief of police administration in the Sarajevo CSB, the Serbian Sarajevo CSB. Could you have a look, please, on the screen again, I'm sorry, at P -- Exhibit P879, which you had a chance to have a look at this morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I cannot see anything on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's going to take a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you have got your folders with you, it's the CSB Romanija-Birac. Sorry ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Page ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 8. We've had this problem before. It won't turn the right way up, will it? All right. Can I -- can we put this on Sanction? ELMO, sorry. Not Sanction. Oh, you can turn it now apparently. No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'll look at it upside down, Mr. Borovcanin. We can see there a basic chart of the CSB in Sarajevo, and the chief was a man named, strangely enough, Zoran Cvijetic. I don't know if it is any relation. I'm not going ask either. Can you tell us, because all we can see underneath that is the SJB chiefs who would report to him, in the hierarchy of the CSB, where would you be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I have a bit of a throat problem. I seem to be catching a cold. Mr. Cvijetic was head of the centre, and within the centre there were several organisational units but, inter alia, the police, "odeljenje" not "uprava," and then there was the department -- the crime department, then also the communications department, the legal administrative department, et cetera. However, in that hierarchy we were all equals, the heads of departments. On this ladder, we were all this -- at the same level. For example, there was the chief of the crime prevention police and then I was head of the uniform police, but we were all at the same level, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So would have you authority to deal with the uniformed police within the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Of course, in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so that we all understand it, the SJB chiefs, we've heard from numerous witnesses, would report to the chief of the CSB. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, that's the way it should be. However, the chiefs of the SJBs were people from the local communities, from the territories of various municipalities. Can I just make a brief comment? They were sort of a bypass between the local authorities and the police. That is to say that they run the public security stations in their areas and quite often, the chiefs of these stations were the -- were candidates who were put forth by political structures, but it is the head of the MUP that made the ultimate decision. As for your question, whether they were -- whether they reported to the chief of the centre according to hierarchy, they were, and that is in accordance with the law and with the rules of service of the police and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was part of your job to inspect the uniformed police section of the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They had police stations. They did not have sections as an "odeljenje." When I speak of myself and the people who worked with me, the inspectors who worked with me, our duty was to act in an instructive fashion in the field, to follow the work of the head of the police station and the policemen as well. We had to look into whether they implemented the law properly, that there was no abuse, whether they ran their stations appropriately, and so on and so forth. That was our duty. From the entrance onwards, we would look at everything very carefully. We would look at everything within the said police station very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you went down to inspect a police station, would you notify the chief of the SJB that you were going make an inspection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, bearing in mind the fact that I was in this line of work before the war as well, it was customary to announce a visit of that kind, for a simple reason. We wouldn't want the local commander or his associates to be absent when we are there. They should be there, by way of supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going look at some of the instructions for inspectors in a moment, but what I want to know is this. Could you -- did you have the authority, from your position, to give orders directly to the uniformed police within the police stations, or did you have to go through the chief of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, my work was just part of the organisational unit in the centre, as I have already said. I could not make any orders independently without previously consulting the chief of the centre who, in turn, reported to the MUP about that. Also, I could not issue orders to the public security station chiefs in the field. I could not do it directly. The procedure and the protocol involved were a well-known thing. If there is something that is of broader interest, namely that a particular communication should be sent to every police station, then usually that kind of information would reach the MUP, and then the chief of the centre would say, Prepare this or prepare that, on that basis. That is how things worked. We were just part of this chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now we're going to see when we look at some of the reports either done by you personally or some of your inspectors that there was dissatisfaction with some of the SJBs. I want to ask you about one aspect of this. If you discovered through your inspection that police officers had been committing crimes and that the SJB chief was not doing anything, would it be your obligation to report that to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: If we had knowledge to that effect, then, yes, certainly. After all, that is our obligation according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to take you in a moment to some documents, but one other thing. You've told us you were not aware of the separation of the MUP at the end of March, beginning of April. Did you ever, before you attended -- before you became part of the Romanija-Birac CSB, did you ever attend any meetings to do with the separation of the MUPs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, perhaps the terminology is not the best. Possible separation or something like that. Perhaps the best explanation would be that there was a total confusion and there was a lack of understanding of the situation. Stories were bandied about. You know what it was like. There was this collective psychosis in town, and so on and so forth. And, of course, people were worried about their very own destinies. I, for one, wondered what on earth was going on. I couldn't believe what was happening, and I was in the police. Once I attended meeting - you asked me about that - at the Serbia hotel, at Ilidza. As far as I'm concerned, I attended that meeting spontaneously. We were playing football and then we were talking a bit and then we just sort of spontaneously said, Let's meet up and let's discuss all of this at a meeting. The situation was very confusing in the MUP. There were many changes, personnel changes in the MUP. We ordinary people did not really understand that. Every reorganisation of any kind should be accompanied by legal documents but there weren't any legal documents, when this separation of the MUP happened or whatever term you're use.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't know what you'd call it, but do you agree there was the original MUP, to which you had belonged, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and when you were in the CSB Romanija-Birac, there was the MUP of the Serbian Republic, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. But then two MUPs came into being. The federal MUP and the MUP of Republika Srpska. This went hand in hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were the -- the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, was an ex-member of the Bosnian MUP, is that right, republican MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: All of us were members of the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this meeting in the Hotel Serbia which, as you say, you told the investigator about, give us a rough idea of, please, when that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that it was March. I cannot tell you the exact date with any certainty. But it must have been March. Say mid-March? But I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you say it was a spontaneous meeting as you were playing football. Can I ask, how many of you attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, there were a few of my inspectors there, my former colleagues, because when I worked in the -- in the inspectorate of the republican SUP, we went out for recreation together, so a few of these inspectors. And when we went down there, we found Mr. Mandic there, Momo Mandic, and Cedo Kljajic, I think. And the investigator asked me whether Mr. Mico was there. I was not sure. I thought that he wasn't there, actually, and even now I think that he wasn't there, that that is more likely. And Kovac, I don't know whether he was there or not. But I cannot say that with any degree of certainty. I don't want to say anything for sure that I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's Tomo Kovac you're talking about, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At that time he was, I think -- no, I don't think. I know that he was the chief of the public security station of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying -- I'm sorry -- are you saying that Momo Mandic and Cedo Kljajic were playing football with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Not Momo Mandic, but Cedo Kljajic was, yes. He liked it. He would come to play football. Other colleagues did too. Cedo Tosic might have been there as well. I can't remember, believe me. Dusko Ivanovic, for instance. I know that we liked to play ball. We liked to play football.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But then how was it that Momo Mandic turned up at this spontaneous meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, somebody said that there would be a gathering of sorts there. I did not know, I hadn't received an invitation or anything, so we went primarily out of curiosity to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you got there, what was going on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, if we look at it from a professional point of view, this really was not serious enough to be a police gathering. Some people were standing by the bar chatting, others were sitting elsewhere, so there was nothing really important. It wasn't that there was a serious discussion going on. We were simply talking about what would happen, whether there would be a war, whether there would not be a war. Everything was sort of hanging in the air, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You call this -- you yourself call this a meeting, so it wasn't just people sitting over a drink was it? It was a proper meeting, even though you had had nobody taking minutes and no agenda.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. There was no written invitation, there was nothing. Some of our colleagues said that Momo or whoever would be at the Serbia hotel and let's go and see what's going on. So it was really spontaneous. I didn't even know who would be there. There weren't too many of us anyway. That's only meeting that I know of -- or, actually, the only one that I attended, the only one of its kind. And it remained unfinished, as it were, because we did not leave it any wiser than when we had arrived there actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But talking about what would happen, whether there would be a war, did you or didn't you discuss the departure of the Serbian members of the MUP from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: There weren't any concrete talks or concrete names. Quite simply, solutions were being sought. That's the way I see it. Personally I was very curious as a policeman but I could not say anything more about that. Sometimes my neighbours wondered too. They said, You're supposed to know about all of this. You work for the police. I don't know. Well, maybe I'm just not a good policeman. That's what I would tell them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. So you say there was no concrete talk or concrete names but was there, if you like, a general discussion about the departure of the Serbian police officers from the joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Not about separation but the basic message from that meeting was be careful, see where your families are. If people have a bypass of sorts, if they have relatives in villages, whatever, perhaps it would be a good idea to take care of your wives and children. That is the general drift of what was being said but nothing was agreed specifically at that meeting. I claim with full responsibility that no agreement was reached at that meeting nor were we ordered at that meeting to do anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look, I will tell you one more time, Mr. Borovcanin. You told us that reasonably senior at least two police officers that can you name were present at that meeting; Mandic, who was the assistant minister, and Cedo Kljajic, whose position I have forgotten. Now are you saying what was discussed was your families and children?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, among other things, there's nothing more precious than your family, if we are to be honest. I was very concerned about my own wife and children, like all the other colleagues, and it was not unusual to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll -- as you know, we're going to have a look at the minutes of the meeting of July the 11th at which you were present. Because one of the things that is referred to by Zupljanin is right at the beginning: "It seems a long time since we met in Sarajevo ..." Was Zupljanin present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: You mean the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the Hotel Serbia in March.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: -- in June or in July?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Was Zupljanin present at this meeting in the Hotel Serbia in March?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's move on. I want you now, please, to have a look at some documents. First of all, a list of instructions, which is 65 ter 2400. It's -- sorry, it takes a little bit of time to come up on the screen. Now, this is -- it's called an inspection checklist. You may or may not have had this particular copy of this document, but were you familiar with the contents, as to what had to happen on an inspection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, if you had asked me that question without the image, I probably would not have remembered. But there's nothing out of the ordinary here. It's just the reminder, a checklist for inspection. But as far as I know, in one part of the crime investigation service, you have this checklist to make sure that you sort of look at all the items when inspecting a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But that's what I mean, you're familiar with -- the things that -- I'll start this question again, I'm sorry. Those matters contained there, are those the standard procedures when carrying out a check? Inspection, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I have a lot of experience in this job, and this checklist is a bit terse. That was -- it was scant. At the beginning, we did not have all the prerequisites well established, such as records, logistics and all the things that you need to do your work properly. This reminder, this checklist, was developed by experienced people but it's not quite complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: A police checklist would have been much -- much more complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this is apparently a police checklist. Do you mean your own checklist?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No. No, that's not in dispute. This is an inspection checklist. That's true. I just mean to say that this is more in the line of work of the crime investigation service. If you look at all the set of items that need to be looked into.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I'm with you. All right. The only other thing I want to point out, if you go, please, in English, to the second page, and also in the B/C/S version. "Upon completion of the inspection, a written report is to be compiled based on the situation found, with positive qualities ... failures noted, and measures and instructions recommended ..." Again, was that a -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just finish this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that a standard procedure? That's all I want to know. Please, just yes or no. And then we'll deal with Mr. Pantelic's correction.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
