utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just informed by Ms. Savic that actually the English translation of that particular document, the heading is not corresponding to B/C/S version. So maybe we could hear from witness what is the exact title of B/C/S version of that document and then we could later on ask interpreter service to make corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to page 1 in B/C/S and could you just read out the -- what it actually says there in Serbian language and then we'll get an interpretation. Sorry, Mr. Borovcanin, can you just read out what it says there, at the top of this document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: All right. Reminder for instructive supervision.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, this is a literal translation. The translation provided in English is very reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you, Ms. Savic. Thank you very much. Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P988, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe for identification at this stage and then if official translation will rectify this, the title or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I heard the interpreter say that was a reasonable interpretation, through my earphones, the way it's been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SAVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I cannot see any reason to have it retranslated. It's pretty obvious what it is, whatever it is headed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I myself wouldn't have seen a difference. But the -- in any event, Mr. Pantelic's reservation about it being exhibited at this point, whatever it is called, it's the essence of the document on which the Prosecution is relying, so I see no problem with it being exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pantelic, what is the inference that you would wish to draw from the possible difference in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, I really don't want to -- to sort of split hair but it's just my suggestion that maybe this -- this translation should be corrected, or if it is okay, at this stage I don't have any problem with it at all. It is up to our interpreters and the translation unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean, Your Honours have admitted it and marked it now so -- as Your Honours rightly say, it is the content I'm concerned with, not the title.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to look at some of the inspections, as I say, you carried out, but to keep this chronological, I'm going ask you to look at the minutes of the meeting of the 11th of July in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is P160, please. Actually, I'm sorry, I've made a mistake, sorry, because if I keep it chronological, there's an earlier document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at document which is 65 ter 397, which is a report, which is an inspection. This, I think, if we look at the last page in both English and B/C/S, it's three page -- third page in B/C/S and fourth page in English, this is a report done by you. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That's correct. Myself and my colleague, Milomir Orasanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if we go back, please, to the second page both in the English and B/C/S - and we need to go down a bit, yeah, thank you - 27th and 28th of May. At that stage you're still an inspector. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you inspect Vogosca and Ilijas SJB. And you say: "In the area of" -- one, two, third paragraph under Vogosca: "In the area of the station, there are two main check-points controlled by employees of the police station, while the secondary entrances into town are being controlled by the Serbian Territorial Defence." Who did you mean by "the Serbian Territorial Defence"? Are we talking about army or paramilitary or what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The army, definitely. The Territorial Defence is part of the armed forces. It was, in the former Yugoslavia. And it was still, when the army of the Republika Srpska was established. The Territorial Defence was then part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you point out that there are personnel issues which we needn't trouble you with, and you propose various appointments. You --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to go, sorry, to the third page in English, and still the second page in B/C/S. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You actually propose people there. So you had the authority, did you, to suggest appointments, even though the appointments had to be made by the minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: You said it right. We were just proposing, and the decision was made by the minister. That is, the head of centre, with the approval of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on Ilijas, I just want to ask you about one matter. It's on the last page in the B/C/S and in the English. Again, there are problems, but you say: "A small unit for special purposes has been established in the police station. It was stressed that it had equipment shortages in armour." Was this a special police unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: At that time, and these were the early days, if we're looking at the Ilijas municipality, which was, militarily speaking, inside a horseshoe, there were very frequent exchanges of fire. And in that period, one of those young men, unfortunately dead now, was a member of the special detachment of the republic SUP and since he happened to be there, during the war he organised this small unit of young men, simply like some assault task force to defend this immediate area, the citizens, the neighbourhood. It was a spontaneous move without any orders from above. People were making decisions as they went, played it by the ear, decisions that they thought right for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But this shouldn't have happened, should it, without an order, from what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I would agree with you completely, if we had been able to make at least a telephone call to Vogosca and other stations at the time, let alone other communications. It was simply impossible to go somewhere for an inspection. I myself was targeted by target -- by sniper fire at least three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to come onto communications as a separate topic, but I -- I'm sorry. This was something that you had to report because it was a breach of -- of police orders, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't understand why it would be a violation. It was a part of the police reserve, whereas special units, as you call them, were made up of young people. It was a mix of active duty and the reserve force. But reservists normally served at police stations even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but I thought we -- I'm sorry. We seem to be going backwards now. I thought we'd agreed that you needed an order before you could set up a special purposes unit and that didn't happen. I'm simply asking you whether you the reason you reported that to your superiors was because it shouldn't have happened without an order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I can't agree with you on this. The real answer is that we were unable to inform them. How are we to report to the MUP or ask for their approval if we didn't receive any original reports? In this report, we are discussing the existing situation, and the people had organised themselves. When I say "people," I mean the police. It was a matter of necessity, you must understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then what was the purpose of telling -- of agreeing with me - and you started it - by saying that this should not have happened without an order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: And when did I say that? When did I agree with you? Maybe we did not understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's clear this up. What you said a minute ago - let's just go back over this - was -- I asked you about this special purposes unit. I asked you: "Was this a special police unit?" And you said: "At that time, and they were the early days, if we're looking at the Ilijas municipality, which was, militarily speaking, inside a horseshoe ... and then one of those young men, unfortunately now dead, was a member of the special detachment of the SUP ... he happened to be there ... he organised a small unit of young men ... it was a spontaneous move without any orders from above." And I then -- I then put to you or asked you: "That shouldn't have happened," not there" which is what is recorded in the transcript, "should it, without an order, from what you are saying?" "I would agree with you completely, if we had been able to make at least a telephone to Vogosca," and so on. Now, do you agree -- sorry. I thought you were saying, as we've understood it, you cannot set up a Special Police unit without an order either from the CSB chief or above. Now, is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to be clearer now. If we had been able to communicate with them and if they had been able to ask us, Are you intending to do this and that? Of course, we would have asked for their approval. But I'm repeating again. We could not have obtained approval from the ministry or the centre if we had no such knowledge. We did not have any knowledge that this unit had been established until my colleague and I arrived on the spot. That's a fact. I'm not denying that communications were working but I'm not deciding the rest. The rest is on a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Well, tell me if this is right, so we all sing from the same hymn sheet. You didn't know that the Special Police unit had been established until you went to do your inspection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You should -- or somebody in the CSB should have known about it, if the proper procedures were being followed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: You see, MUP was -- is -- was in the process of organising itself. Those were the early days. Please try to understand that. How were we to take preventive steps before this unit was formed if we had no communication with them? That is the point. And this applies not only to that station. There will be -- we'll come back to this. I believe there will be other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was -- you could get to Ilijas to make this inspection. What was to prevent Ilijas seeking permission? Or the chief in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Maybe he could have gotten into his car and come. But there was another aspect. The exchanges of fire happened every day. That's maybe one thing that you keep overlooking. This police station was in a war-affected zone. Maybe policemen had no time for things like that. It was May. Only later, when the system was in place and when the communications were safer, were we able to visit each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we've done this topic to death.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just go to the front page again of both, the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Handwritten at the top is: "For the chief, Milos Zuban." Do you know whose writing that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know whose handwriting it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just tell the Court, who was Milos Zuban?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Milos Zuban was, at that time, at the seat of THE MUP in Bijeljina. And if my memory serves me well, I think he was either chief of the police administration or perhaps a head of one department within the police administration. There was a sort of musical chairs game going on, so I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can we move on to what is the next document in time that I want to show you and that is the minutes of the meeting of the 11th of July, P160.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I should have asked -- can I please have that admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P989, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this meeting you did attend, because we'll see your name later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just looking at my note.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, to page -- just to identify your presence ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In the English, it's page - oh, golly - 16. And in the B/C/S, all I can say is ... I can't say very much. I'm told it's got the ERN number at the top, 1869, but I don't know that can be right. Sorry, I asked somebody to -- because I can't read Cyrillic, Your Honour, I asked somebody to mark it up, and I'm not sure it has been marked up. Can we have 1865 at the top, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that you? I haven't the faintest idea. Is that you, sir? Is that you, Mr. Borovcanin, we see on that page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I want do go back, please, and now that we've identified you being there, to the beginning when Stojan Zupljanin spoke, and this is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In English, it's page 5 of 29 at the bottom. And in B/C/S, it's the fourth -- fifth page. B/C/S, Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zupljanin -- first of all, as Mico Stanisic was there, do you know why Stojan Zupljanin opened the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know that. It's not usual that somebody except that the minister should open it, but I can't think of a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, I don't know what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's misleading. It's misleading because Mico Stanisic opened this meeting, not Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question should been: Do you know why he spoke first, Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't see anything unusual there. This is a flexible approach to a meeting in general. Maybe the minister wanted to hear everyone out and then to make a summary at the end. That would be customary too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I said, he starts off by saying: "It has been a long time since the last meeting in Sarajevo and a lot of things have changed ... then." Do you know to what meeting in Sarajevo he was referring?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Are you talking about Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about Stojan Zupljanin. In front of you it has Stojan Zupljanin's speech and it begins: "It has been a long time since the last meeting in Sarajevo and a lot of things have changed since then." Now, to what meeting in Sarajevo was he referring? Because it's addressed to everybody who was present.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I really don't know about that. Probably I didn't even attend the meeting that is being mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But you were asked to attend this meeting and you told us about a meeting in the Hotel Serbia. You have no idea to what he was referring?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And why was it that you were asked to attend this meeting? Because Mr. Cvijetic was there as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That's right. I assume that I would be invited to that meeting because, after all, we were supposed to meet. I repeat once again that there weren't that many meetings of this kind at first, so it was an opportunity for us to get to know each other, to know who was doing what, and probably the top people who were in charge made an assessment, to the effect that I should attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You see, the majority of the other people there were -- well, actually -- no. Don't worry about that. I'm sorry, no. Forget that. Now, can we go, please, in the English to page 8 of 29, and in the B/C/S to page 5, which is 1855 at the top. This is still Zupljanin speaking. And he is talking about the army Crisis Staff wartime Presidency demand gathering as many Muslims as possible and leave such non-defined camps to the internal affairs. The conditions in these camps are poor. There is no food. Some individuals do not comply with international standards, because, among other things, the concentration centres are not appropriate. Now, were you aware, from your own knowledge, by July of 1992, that people were being kept in collection centres, non-Serbs, which were being staffed by police officers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: What you're asking me about is something that I first heard of at that meeting when Mr. Zupljanin was speaking. I certainly hadn't heard of it before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So any inspections you had carried out or any reports had not mentioned that within the area of responsibility of the CSB Sarajevo, there were collection centres which were being staffed by members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: First of all, these collection centres, as we call them, were under the Army of Republika Srpska. In any war, there are such population movements, these demographic migrations that are very vigorous. And, well, the centres were under the Army of Republika Srpska and if sometimes the police would provide security at these camps, perhaps the answer would be that there weren't enough men, and we were - how should I put this? - someone who would protect people at a particular locality so that nothing would happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Which facilities are you thinking of that were under the control of the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I don't know specifically what localities they were. When the investigator asked me about this, I said that, unfortunately, I learned of a great many things from the media. For a long time, we were not dealing with that at all. I mean, we couldn't follow everything, 25 police stations. In these times of chaos, when communications were broken off. It was very difficult to follow other things as well. However, let me say that once again, if a group of citizens would appear somewhere, what could we do? We were there possibly to take them to a particular place, to protect them. That's how I see it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But -- sorry. You said these collection centres were under the command of the army which is not what Zupljanin is saying at all. He is saying non-defined camps are being left to the police. Now, in your area of responsibility, were you aware of such camps or collection centres?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: At that time, most definitely not. If -- if they existed at all, and if the MUP had anything to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was the -- the SJB at Pale within your area of responsibility for inspections and the like?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When the centre was constituted. Or, rather, when the service was established, the one that I headed. Then this was under our authority. Up until then, well, I don't know. I worked as an inspector, and I carried out inspections. So how should I put this? Without any particular appointment, as it were. I was just an inspector in a centre that was still undergoing the process of its establishment. It was still in the making. Can you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By July of 1992 your centre was established, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever send inspectors to Pale, or go yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you know what? Since the police station of Pale is relatively nearby, and regardless of where you wanted to go out into the field, there is no way of avoiding it. So it's on the way. And we would unofficially stop there. And we would in this way find out about other police stations that we had not known about, whether they were properly organised, whether they were properly manned, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going ask you very briefly then to look, please, at a photograph of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is R093 -- that's the ERN. 65 ter, no idea. Oh, yeah, sorry. I can -- it's 65 ter 10278. Your Honours, this is one of the photographs that was taken in the sort of massive photographic sweep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you had a chance to look at this this morning. Can you just, again, using the pen that you had this morning --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thanks. That's fine. No, no, it's the wrong one. Oh, I see, we're looking at it upside down. Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just indicate where the SJB was in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you mark that with a 1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was there a building called the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. This was a building where meetings were held from time to time, concerts, and the like, then dances, social gatherings. Yes, yes, that building did exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you mark that as well, please, and put a 2 by it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever become aware of non-Serbs being detained by the police from Pale in the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I learned about that only later. Then, no. I had no occasion to see these people or to get any direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would the SJB in Pale, however, have been obliged to report to Mr. Cvijetic that they were holding people in the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, that would be according to the rules, I think. At least that's what I think, that that is it how the information should have come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because it wasn't an authorised prison, was it, like Kula in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No, no. That's how I see it. People who had fled from some war zones in the area, I assume that that's it, or people who fled simply out of fear from what might happen in the future. They came there, and I suppose that the police protected them, so that they could be safely transported to the separation line, which, later, did happen, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you knew nothing about it, what makes you think that people who had fled were being placed there by the police for their own protection, as opposed to any other reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, everyone was at a distance from these people. The army, according to the Law on Total National Defence, was not supposed to take care of them. Then it was easiest to give this hot potato to the police, and we simply worked on that. We simply wanted these people to be safe and properly transported to the separation line. That's it. The role of the MUP is not significant at all, in some context -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So whatever you heard about it later, you never heard that anybody had been taken there against their will, and whilst they were there, beaten up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you had known, if you had done an inspection, or you had sent an inspector, and you had found that people were being kept there against their will, is that something you would have reported?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: That goes without saying. It would be our official duty not only to report to our immediate superior in the Ministry of the Interior but also we'd have to inform the military command. After all, there was a war going on. In all wars, anywhere in the world, there were collection centres. There were camps. That is a necessity. That is a product of war. The military had to bear that in mind. That's way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that may be a suitable moment to pause, although I have a couple of more questions on the July the 11th meeting. May I asking that photograph of Pale be admitted and marked, please. In fact, we'd better have two. I suppose one that was marked one and a plain one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The un-annotated photograph will be Exhibit P990, and the annotated one will be Exhibit P991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as we indicated earlier, sir, we will now excuse you until tomorrow. You are not released as a witness, and I am required to enjoin you not to discuss your testimony -- not to speak with lawyers on other side of the matter or to discuss your testimony with anybody outside the courtroom. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00, in this courtroom, and the Court is not rising at this moment. The Usher will now escort you from the -- from the Chamber. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall abide by these rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Your Honours deal with the matters I have raised, I have in addition been reminded, if I ever knew it, that all the orders made in respect of Stanisic by the decision of the 26th November 2008 apply to the Zupljanin Defence. Accordingly, the rule is, at the moment: "The Defence shall not approach a witness or potential witness identified by the Prosecution without prior written notice to the Prosecution, in order to allow the Prosecution to obtain the consent of the witness and to take steps as may be necessary and appropriate to protect the security and privacy of the witness or potential witness." That was the 6th June 2005 decision which then applied to Stanisic only, but by the 26th of November 2008 order also applies to Zupljanin. May I say straightaway, I fully think that, probably Mr. Krgovic, like me, wasn't aware of it, and possibly either Mr. Pantelic either. But that is the situation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. So we need say nothing further on that issue at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the other two matters raised by Ms. Korner at the beginning of today's session, the first has to do with whether the three pages which she sought to have marked and entered as an exhibit could and should be so entered. And we are reminded of the proceedings of the 18th of February, and this matter, as far as the Chamber is concerned, has been dealt with. And the -- there is no dispute -- there appears to be no dispute as to the accuracy of the -- transcript that was verbally put to the witness by Ms. Korner in her -- in her questions, and therefore the necessity of and the propriety of admitting the three pages separately as exhibits does not arise. As regards the second matter, and that is the way in which the list of what we would refer to as recently discovered or recently uncovered or recently realised to be of assistance documents. That is, and counsel would appreciate, a matter which has -- which continues to be raised, and it is an issue which the Chamber will not rule on today, because it is a matter that is under active consideration. So with that, we take the adjournment to tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just on the point of view of interviews being put to witnesses. Just for future reference, if either we put it to, let's say, to Defence witness or for various reasons we put part of an interview to the witness, the normal procedure would be that it becomes an exhibit simply so there cannot be any argument about the accuracy. But if you're saying it is read out accurately, then no exhibit. In fact, I did skip various parts but they don't really matter. I'll accept that, but I just want to know for future reference. So provided we read the whole thing out, no exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This was -- this was Mr. Hannis's own proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. I'm not sure that's correct, but ... anyhow. All right. I heard Your Honour say case-by-case basis, but, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
